023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questi: James Bond is the British secret agent Ian Fleming created in 1953, known worldwide through the film series running since 1962 for its gadgets, glamour, and globe-trotting villains. Behind the martini and the license to kill lie serious questions: whether a hedonist can face death, what Plato's rulers would make of MI6, whether Bond is a Nietzschean overman or just a well-dressed animal, and how the rule of law survives a man who kills for queen and country.
024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guarante: In 2005, Princeton philosopher Harry Frankfurt's slim essay On Bullshit — a technical analysis of speechmakers who simply don't care whether what they say is true — unexpectedly spent months on the bestseller list. This book asks why that struck such a nerve, from the Iraq war's weapons claims to fabricated memoirs and product placement disguised as conversation. Its essays test, defend, and extend Frankfurt's definition, asking when bullshit is tolerable, how it differs from lying, and why philosophy itself may be our best defense against it.
025 - The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothi: The Beatles are the Liverpool quartet who became the most famous band in history, setting off Beatlemania in the 1960s and transforming popular music. This book treats their rise alongside Bob Dylan and Elvis Presley as a case study in how novelty enters culture: whether meaning is created rather than found, how the body's feelings drive what the mind thinks, whether Beatlemania was a genuine religious phenomenon, and how an artist's sense of destiny can make its own truth.
026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger: South Park is the gleefully vulgar animated satire that Comedy Central has run since 1997, following four Colorado boys through episodes that mock politicians, religions, and celebrities alike. The show was accused of corrupting the young for reasons strikingly like those that got Socrates executed. Its essays use Cartman, the Chewbacca Defense, and the theology of the show's over-the-top plots to teach logic, probe the problem of evil, question relativism, and ask why bad reasoning drives real laws and beliefs.
027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M: Alfred Hitchcock, the 'Master of Suspense' who directed from the 1920s to the 1970s, gave cinema Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window, and The Birds. His contributors argue the films are organized around ideas: Rope stages a botched Nietzschean superman's murder, Psycho poses the problem of horrendous evil, Shadow of a Doubt teaches the difference between belief and knowledge, and The Birds tests whether romantic love is worth its costs. Watching Hitchcock, we learn, means confronting how little we can know for certain.
028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy -: The Grateful Dead were the San Francisco band at the heart of the 1960s counterculture, famous for never playing a song the same way twice and for a fan community, the Deadheads, that followed them from 1965 until Jerry Garcia's death in 1995. Their parking-lot markets, taping ethos, and Buddhist-tinged lyrics raise real questions: what makes a community, whether capitalism can care, who owns an improvised performance, and how a grinning skeleton became a guide to life and death.
029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy -: Quentin Tarantino is the American director of Reservoir Dogs, Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill, and Death Proof, celebrated and criticized for stylized violence and endless talk about pop culture. His criminals argue about tipping, foot massages, and whether a bullet that missed was a miracle — and the films ask whether even hitmen live by a morality. Essays draw on Nietzsche, Hume, and Rawls to ask whether revenge can be justified, and whether watching it all is corrupted spectatorship or something deeper.
030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Carefu: Pink Floyd, the English band formed in 1965, turned psychedelic experiment into monumental concept albums — The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals, The Wall — meditations on time, money, madness, and alienation. Their songs interrogate the schools that indoctrinate us, the markets and states of Animals' beast fable, and the industry that commodifies artists. Was founder Syd Barrett's madness the price of art, and was the band punk before punk existed?
031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The B: Johnny Cash, the 'Man in Black,' was country music's great outlaw conscience, famous for prison concerts at Folsom and San Quentin, gospel hymns, and songs of murderers, drifters, and working men. He was also, as Kris Kristofferson said, a walking contradiction: an addict and a devout Christian. His songs ask what an authentic self is when the persona was manufactured, what makes work meaningful, what makes a law unjust, and how evil fits a world made by a benevolent God.
032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy -: Bruce Springsteen, 'The Boss,' has since the 1970s been America's foremost rock chronicler of working-class life, from Born to Run to Born in the U.S.A. to The Rising. His songs of factories, failed promises, and hard-won hope raise questions philosophers usually save for books: whether he is a prophet or merely a poet, what Marx would make of his characters, whether encores are gifts or obligations, and how a flag-wrapped protest song can be a lesson in democracy.
